raw_case_text: A 41-year-old Sudanese woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever (39.5 C) associated with fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. Clinical evaluation and a blood test revealed a diagnosis of malaria, for which treatment was administered. During the next few days, her symptoms worsened, in addition to yellow sclera and low hemoglobin (5.5 g/dL) and platelets (43 cells/mL). The patient was transferred to our rheumatology department at Omdurman Military Hospital for further evaluation. Clinical findings were normal except for jaundice (bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL). She indicated that her sister had Behcet's disease. Upon admission, she developed a severe headache associated with confusion and fever, her blood pressure was unrecordable, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9/15. The rapid-response team was called, and she was admitted to a high-dependency unit, where she received six units of fresh frozen plasma, two pools red blood cells, and kept under close observation. After her condition had stabilized, laboratory investigations were requested (Table 1). A diagnosis of SLE and TTP was made, and she was given imipenem 500 mg, acyclovir 75 mg, electrolyte correction, IV normal saline 0.9%, skin and bladder care (five sessions of plasmapheresis), and methylprednisolone 1 g pulse for 3 days, followed by prednisolone 1 mg/kg in a tapering manner. A few days later, after the infection had been controlled, the patient received four doses of rituximab 375 mg/week with caution. Two weeks later, she was discharged in good general condition, with normal results on complete blood count and renal function testing. She was discharged on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg, azathioprine 50 mg, prednisolone 10 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg, calcium supplement 500 mg, and omega 3. On review at two weeks, she was completely well without any complaints.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female presenting with high-grade fever, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting for two days, complicated by progressive jaundice, severe headache, confusion, and shock.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 41-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever (39.5 °C), fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. She was evaluated at an outside clinic, diagnosed with an infection, and received treatment. Over subsequent days, her symptoms worsened with scleral icterus and severe bicytopenia, prompting transfer to the rheumatology department. Upon admission, she acutely developed severe headache, disorientation (GCS 9/15), high fever, and unrecordable blood pressure, requiring emergency medical resuscitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sister has Behçet's disease. Resident of Sudan.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, nausea, vomiting, severe headache, confusion, and jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: Deeply jaundiced sclerae, profound hypotension with unrecordable blood pressure, high fever, Glasgow Coma Scale score 9/15, and clinical shock requiring rapid response team activation.
objective.routine_investigations: Marked hemolytic anemia with hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL and severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 43 cells/μL (43,000/mm^3). Total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL. Autoimmune and microangiopathy evaluation confirmed systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute malaria precipitating systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and secondary thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) with multi-organ crisis (neurological depression GCS 9, circulatory shock, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia). Blood film and clinical evaluation at initial emergency presentation confirmed malaria, for which antiparasitic therapy was administered.
Plan & Outcome: Resuscitated in the High Dependency Unit with 6 units of fresh frozen plasma, 2 units of packed red blood cells, IV normal saline 0.9%, electrolyte correction, and broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage (imipenem 500 mg, acyclovir 75 mg). Treated with five sessions of plasmapheresis and pulse IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg tapering). Following infectious control, received four weekly doses of rituximab (375 mg/m^2). Full clinical recovery achieved; discharged on day 14 on hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine, low-dose prednisolone, and supportive medications with normal CBC and renal function at 2-week follow-up.
